title: Precedence scheduling below factor four
formal:
Does there exist a constant \(\delta\in(0,1)\) and a uniform polynomial-time approximation algorithm for nonpreemptive precedence-constrained scheduling on identical parallel machines whose approximation factor is \(4-\delta\)?

An instance \(I\) gives \(n\ge1\) jobs, \(m\ge1\) identical machines, positive integer processing times \(p_j\), positive integer weights \(w_j\), and an acyclic precedence graph on the jobs. All integers are binary encoded and the entire instance is available before scheduling. The algorithm must return a feasible schedule \(S\) satisfying
\[\mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}(S)]\le(4-\delta)\operatorname{OPT}(I),\qquad \operatorname{cost}(S)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_jC_j.\]
The expectation is only over the algorithm's internal randomness. A deterministic algorithm qualifies. The same \(\delta\) and algorithm must work for every instance, including arbitrary machine counts, processing times and precedence graphs.

This is the algorithmic improvement explicitly requested in Section 4.10 of the 2016 source, with the standard integer input model and randomized expected-cost convention made explicit. It is a historical, resolved target; the source does not ask here for determination of the best possible approximation factor.
why: Precedence constraints can make early completion of a high-weight job depend on processing many low-weight predecessors, while limited parallel capacity creates an additional conflict. Breaking the factor-four guarantee showed that these two effects need not impose the loss in the older approximation analysis. The target was a central scheduling approximation question, and its later resolution is the reason this completed record is inactive.
status_note: Reviewed on 2026-09-14. The 2016 request to improve factor four matches Shi Li’s published FOCS 2017 Theorem 1, with ratio 2+2 ln 2+epsilon for every fixed positive epsilon, and its 2020 journal publication. Model definitions and the full-version Section 6 discussion of super-polynomial horizons were checked. The review establishes a source-matched published resolution, not independent verification of every proof or an existing Lean formalization.

sentences: The historical question asks for a polynomial-time approximation strictly better than factor four for precedence-constrained scheduling.
All jobs must run without interruption on identical machines, and the objective weights the completion time of each job.
The number of machines and arbitrary positive processing times are part of the input.
Shi Li’s 2017 result achieves a factor of about 3.387 plus any fixed positive slack for this general model.
That published improvement resolves the stated target, so the completed record is retained in the inactive archive.

definitions:
Jobs are labelled \(1,\ldots,n\), machines \(1,\ldots,m\), and the precedence input is an explicitly listed directed acyclic graph with endpoints encoded as job indices. An edge \(i\to j\) requires completion of \(i\) before \(j\) starts. All implications along directed paths also follow. No special structure such as a chain, tree or bounded width is promised.

A feasible schedule assigns each job a machine \(a_j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and a nonnegative rational start time \(s_j\). The job occupies that machine throughout \([s_j,s_j+p_j)\), and its completion time is \(C_j=s_j+p_j\). Two intervals on the same machine must be disjoint, and every precedence edge must satisfy \(C_i\le s_j\). All jobs must be scheduled once. Jobs cannot be interrupted, divided among machines or moved after starting; all machines have unit speed and process at most one job at a time. Idle time is allowed. There are no release dates beyond time zero, no online arrivals and no extra machines or faster processors for the algorithm.

The schedule's objective is the sum of its completion times weighted by the supplied \(w_j\). It is not the maximum completion time or the sum of start times. \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the minimum of this objective over all feasible schedules for the same instance and resources. This minimum exists: a schedule can be shifted to earliest feasible starts after fixing its machine assignments and each machine's job order, and there are finitely many such choices. Integer processing times then permit integer start times for an optimum. Positive processing times and weights make \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).

Let \(B\) be the bit length of the explicit instance encoding. A permitted randomized algorithm is one fixed multitape Turing machine with independent fair random bits, finite rational output encoding, and expected running time at most \((B+1)^k+k\) for some fixed positive integer \(k\) on every input. It terminates almost surely and every terminating output must be feasible. Its approximation guarantee holds in expectation separately for each fixed input; no distribution on instances is assumed. A deterministic polynomial-time machine is a special case. Polynomial dependence on the numerical values of the processing times, rather than on their binary lengths, is insufficient.

The improvement \(\delta\) is a fixed positive constant chosen before the input and independent of all its parameters. A factor tending to four with input size or an improvement only for unit-length jobs does not meet this target. The source's alternative request for a stronger integrality gap concerns a particular relaxation; it is not an extra requirement on a successful algorithmic answer.
answer_criterion: Give an algorithm and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of feasibility, uniform polynomial expected running time in the binary input length, and the displayed expected-cost bound for one fixed \(\delta>0\) on every permitted input. Equivalently, a proof or refutation must settle the displayed existence statement in this model. A mathematical publication establishing the algorithm resolves the research target but does not itself supply a Lean-checked benchmark submission. A bound restricted to a fixed number of machines, unit processing times, or preemptive schedules does not establish the general statement.

context_blocks.text: The 2016 report contrasts the factor-two single-machine frontier with a factor-four guarantee on identical parallel machines. It explicitly requests a better algorithm, rather than merely naming the scheduling objective.

Li’s 2017 Theorem 1 gives a \(2+2\ln 2+\varepsilon\) approximation for arbitrary positive processing times and every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Choosing a sufficiently small fixed \(\varepsilon\) makes this strictly less than four, resolving this target. The theorem for unit processing times has a different, smaller factor and is not needed for this disposition.

The full version defines the nonpreemptive identical-machine model and treats the extension beyond polynomially bounded time horizons in Section 6. Thus the cited result is presented as a polynomial-time approximation for binary numerical inputs, not only a pseudo-polynomial algorithm. That section states the extension and refers to earlier analysis; this review does not independently formalize that argument.
The journal version appeared in 2020. The record preserves the original solved question instead of silently replacing it with the different task of finding an optimal approximation threshold.
